evaluation.positioning_hook: A former street criminal turned megachurch pastor must protect his son, his ministry, and his own hypocrisy when a campus romance and a hidden HIV diagnosis threaten to expose the life he built on grace.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: There is a clear faith-based audience and a built-in redemption promise, but the script’s long sermon-forward structure and heavy didacticism narrow the commercial lane. The emotional engine is legible in Michael and Dan’s father-son arc, yet it plays to a specific audience rather than a broad four-quadrant buyer.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook is understandable: a pastor with a criminal past and a son who falls into sexual sin and HIV crisis. The problem is that the script takes a long time to land on the central dramatic conflict, spending much of its runtime in extended church services and testimony blocks.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Reverend Michael Xhosa has a strong backstory and a real contradiction between his past and present, and Dan has a credible fall-and-redemption arc. Supporting characters like Felicia, Bode Cole, and Craig are functional but mostly serve the message rather than revealing surprising personal engines.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s faith-meets-underworld-to-ministry premise has some specificity, especially with the Zimbabwe/Nigeria/UK/US church network and the prison conversion backstory. But the execution is largely declarative and repetitive, with scenes built around speeches rather than dramatic turns.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The first half is dominated by extended worship, prayer, and testimony sequences that do not materially change the story beat to beat. Momentum improves once Dan’s campus life, HIV diagnosis, and church discipline kick in, but the overall shape remains episodic and sermon-driven.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The combination of a former underworld figure, a transnational church machine, and a son’s moral collapse gives the script a distinct faith-drama identity. Still, the underlying arc is familiar redemption material, and the script rarely finds a fresh dramatic angle that feels inevitable and surprising at once.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The church ecosystem has real texture: branches across countries, councils, ordinations, campus fellowships, testimony culture, and ministry hierarchy. That said, the world is more organizational than sensory; it is described in detail but not always dramatized through conflict or lived-in behavior.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is consistently earnest and devotional, with occasional soap-opera and melodramatic turns. It has a recognizable faith-film register, but not yet a sharply ownable tonal signature beyond its intensity and volume.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Michael’s past, Dan’s collapse, and the church’s hypocrisy suggest deeper material about power, shame, and institutional faith. The script gestures toward that depth, but most of it is stated outright in speeches rather than earned through subtext or contradiction.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The father-son dynamic between Michael and Dan is the core engine, and the Bode/Damilola/Mark/Craig triangle adds some relational friction. Even so, most supporting relationships function as message conduits rather than recurring dramatic systems that generate scenes on their own.

lead_characters.name: Reverend Michael Xhosa
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-50s, Zimbabwean/Nigerian background, Christian pastor, father.
lead_characters.hook: A charismatic church founder with a violent criminal past, Michael has turned himself into a transnational ministry leader who speaks like a revivalist and thinks like a strategist. He is at his most compelling when his public holiness collides with private guilt, especially around his son Dan and the hypocrisy inside the church he built.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Denzel Washington in Fences or Forest Whitaker in The Last King of Scotland: a commanding, morally complicated authority figure who gets to preach, confess, and fracture in public. The role offers a big emotional range, from pulpit charisma to paternal devastation to spiritual conviction.

lead_characters.name: Dan Xhosa
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens to early 20s, university student, Christian, son of a pastor.
lead_characters.hook: Dan is the dutiful pastor’s son who wants to inherit his father’s certainty but is pulled into campus romance, sexual recklessness, and shame. His arc is built around collapse and restoration, and the script gives him the clearest coming-of-age trajectory in the piece.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Timothée Chalamet in Beautiful Boy or Jharrel Jerome in Moonlight a chance to play vulnerability, denial, and spiritual reckoning in one arc. It asks for an actor who can carry innocence, temptation, humiliation, and redemption without losing sympathy.

lead_characters.name: Felicia Abia
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late teens to early 20s, university student, Christian.
lead_characters.hook: Felicia is the campus catalyst: flirtatious, sincere, and ultimately the emotional hinge between Dan’s fall and his later restoration. She disappears for long stretches, but the script positions her as the woman whose choices carry the story’s most consequential private cost.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Teyonah Parris in If Beale Street Could Talk or Jurnee Smollett in Lovecraft Country a chance to play warmth, desire, and moral gravity at once. The part offers a strong emotional pivot and a late reveal that reframes the romance.

lead_characters.name: Pastor Bode Cole
lead_characters.hook: Bode is the polished church operator who talks like a visionary but behaves like a political fixer. He is useful as an institutional antagonist because he understands the language of faith while weaponizing procedure, access, and reputation.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Giancarlo Esposito in Breaking Bad or Jeffrey Wright in Boardwalk Empire a chance to play controlled menace under a calm surface. It offers a sly, authoritative performance with real power in the room.

lead_characters.name: Deaconess Damilola Cole
lead_characters.hook: Damilola is the church matriarch who manages hospitality, protocol, and moral authority with a warm but firm hand. She reads as the stabilizing public face of the institution, even when the private politics around her are anything but stable.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Viola Davis in Fences or Alfre Woodard in Clemency a chance to project authority, grace, and emotional intelligence in the same frame. It’s a grounded, high-trust performance part with real scene-stealing potential.

lead_characters.name: Craig Alli
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens to early 20s, university student, pastor’s son.
lead_characters.hook: Craig is the smooth-talking campus insider who trades in gossip, surveillance, and opportunism. He is the story’s most overtly duplicitous young character, and the script uses him as both comic pressure and institutional sabotage.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Lakeith Stanfield in Atlanta or Shameik Moore in Dope a chance to play charm with a dangerous edge. It’s a fun, slippery part with room for wit, manipulation, and betrayal.

lead_characters.name: Mark Cole
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens to early 20s, university student, church insider.
lead_characters.hook: Mark is the obedient son and rising church insider who becomes useful to the power structure because he is disciplined, ambitious, and easy to deploy. He is less psychologically deep than Dan, but he functions well as the institutional favorite.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave John Boyega in Detroit or Stephan James in If Beale Street Could Talk a chance to play contained intensity and moral pressure. It’s a clean, watchful supporting part with room for resentment and ambition.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: specialty theatrical, faith-based theatrical, or streaming original with church-audience marketing.

budget.note: The church sanctuary, campus, hospital, prison, stadium, and multiple branch settings create a broad but still scopeable footprint; the crowd scenes and choir work are the main cost drivers.

casting.note: The project needs a commanding lead who can preach, confess, and carry long monologues, plus a large supporting ensemble of clergy, students, and congregants with credible regional accents.

development.note: The script is built around extended sermon blocks, repeated scripture exposition, and a very long testimony structure, so the main development question is how much of the material can be dramatized rather than delivered.

comp_set.title: The Apostle
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the pulpit charisma, spiritual fervor, and moral contradiction of a preacher whose public ministry is inseparable from private sin.

comp_set.title: War Room
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the faith-audience lane and the overtly devotional storytelling that treats prayer, testimony, and conversion as the dramatic engine.

comp_set.title: The Blind Side
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on broad inspirational uplift and redemption-through-community, even though this script is more explicitly church-centered.

comp_set.title: The Preacher's Wife
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the faith-forward, family-centered emotional promise and the emphasis on grace as a life-changing force.

audience_target.primary_audience: Faith-based adult audiences who respond to redemption stories, church politics, and testimony-driven drama.
audience_target.demographics: Adults 30+, skewing female but with meaningful male churchgoing appeal; strongest among church-attending audiences in African and diaspora communities.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary settings, large dialogue-heavy ensemble, and a few crowd-heavy church sequences keep this in indie feature territory rather than true microbudget.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals teams building inspirational drama slates
specialty financiers looking for uplift titles with built-in community marketing
lane_fit.detail: The script sits naturally in the church-audience lane: testimony, conversion, family repair, and public redemption are the selling points. Its strongest commercial path is as an inspirational feature with a clear moral promise and a built-in audience that understands the language of the piece.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The church network is broad, but no side character is developed enough on the page to justify a clean sequel or spinoff vector.

strengths.dimension_or_area: A preacher with a criminal past
strengths.what_it_means: That contradiction gives the script a built-in moral engine and a role that could attract a serious actor looking for authority, shame, and redemption in one part. Buyers in the faith-drama lane respond to a lead who can sell both testimony and danger.
strengths.evidence: Michael’s long confession about his street life, prison sentence, conversion, and rise to ministry.

strengths.what_it_means: The Michael/Dan relationship gives the script an emotional throughline that can anchor marketing around family, legacy, and second chances. That makes it legible to church audiences and to actors who want a generational drama rather than a sermon-only piece.
strengths.evidence: Michael’s warnings to Dan at university, Dan’s collapse, the hospital reconciliation, and the final testimony.

strengths.what_it_means: The branches in Zimbabwe, South Africa, the UK, the U.S., and Nigeria create a scalable institutional backdrop that feels bigger than a single congregation. That gives the project a sense of scope and a recognizable diaspora footprint for targeted buyers.
strengths.evidence: The council roll call, branch references, campus fellowship rollout, and international convention scenes.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Faith content with built-in audience behavior
strengths.what_it_means: The script is designed around prayer, testimony, music, and altar-call conversion, which are not just themes but audience participation cues. That makes it commercially useful for faith-based distribution and event-style marketing.
strengths.evidence: Repeated congregational call-and-response, choir numbers, and the final salvation invitation.

whats_special.headline: This is a faith-drama with a real commercial lane: a charismatic, morally compromised pastor, a son’s fall-and-return arc, and a transnational church world that already knows how to market itself. The script’s biggest asset is that it can be sold as both inspirational uplift and actor-driven redemption, with a budget footprint that stays inside indie feature economics.

items.detail: The opening church service runs for pages before the central family conflict fully arrives, and much of that material is prayer, scripture, and testimony rather than scene-level drama. For a buyer, that means the script’s hook is real but delayed, and the pacing will be the first conversation in any greenlight meeting.

items.area: The dialogue often functions as exposition.
items.detail: Characters repeatedly explain the theme of grace, salvation, and church structure in speeches that sound like teaching notes more than dramatized conflict. That keeps the message clear, but it also limits subtext and makes several scenes feel interchangeable.

The campus romance, sexual behavior, HIV diagnosis, and church discipline are all spelled out in long-form testimony and confession, leaving little room for discovery. A producer will notice that the emotional beats are strong but arrive through narration more than dramatic escalation.

items.area: The ensemble is vivid but not equally deep.
items.detail: Bode, Damilola, Craig, Mark, and Felicia all serve clear functions, but only Michael and Dan feel fully built as durable lead-level roles. That matters because the script presents a large church ecosystem, yet most of it is operating as support for the central message rather than as a scene-generating ensemble.

The final stretch jumps into narration about future ministries, marriages, children, and branch expansion instead of dramatizing those outcomes. That gives the story closure, but it also signals that the script is more interested in declaring destiny than earning it on the page.

issues.headline: The main friction is structural: the script spends a lot of time in proclamation mode before it gets to the family-and-fall story that actually carries the movie. Buyers will also notice that the ensemble and ending are more declarative than dramatic, which makes the piece feel message-forward even when the underlying premise is strong.
